newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian PM apologises for "stolen" Aborigines.
newsitem.headline: Australian PM apologises for "stolen" Aborigines.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard made an unexpected personal apology on Monday to tens of thousands of Aborigines forcibly removed from their parents under a past government policy of assimilation.

"Personally, I feel deep sorrow for those of my fellow Australians who suffered injustices under the practices of past generations towards indigenous people," Howard told a major conference on Aboriginal reconciliation.
"I am sorry for the hurt, the trauma, many here today may continue to feel as a consequence of those practices," he said.
Howard received loud applause for his apology, but jeers when he said Australian history since white settlement in 1788 was not a history of "imperialism and exploitation and racism".
Many of the 1,500 Aboriginal and political leaders turned their back on Howard as he continued his speech.
Before his speech, Howard was abused by an angry Aboriginal woman who jumped on stage and harangued both Howard and populist politician Pauline Hanson.
Delegates were told by conference leader Pat Dodson that black and white Australia were at a crossroads.
"We meet at a moment of truth for this nation," said Dodson, chairman of the Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation.
"Reconciliation stands at a crossroad as the nation debates two extremely important issues -- native title and the 'Stolen Generation'," Dodson said.

Australia is currently embroiled in a bitter row over Aboriginal native title on farming land and past forced assimilation of children, a practice labelled genocidal by a human rights report to be released this week.

Tens of thousands of Aboriginal children were taken from their parents from the 1880s to the 1960s to be brought up in children's homes or by white parents. Those children are called the "Stolen Generation" or "People of the Bleaching".
Australia's Human Rights Commission and Aboriginal leaders have called the assimilation policy genocidal and called for the government to formally apologise to Aborigines.
In a poignant opening ceremony, Howard and other political leaders presented smouldering grass and twigs piled on pieces of bark to Aboriginal elders at the conference.
The ceremony represented acknowledgment that Aborigines were traditional owners of the land and was a symbolic invitation for white leaders to be their guests at the conference.
Howard looked uncomfortable as he sat and listened to official opening speech.
"The 10-point (Howard native title) plan...is not acceptable," said Dodson, earning a standing ovation.
Dodson also called on the government to compensate those Aborigines taken away from their parents.

"We can compensate for forcing people to hand in their guns and we now have to find a way to compensate those who were taken away (from parents)," said Dodson, referring to gun laws introduced after last year's mass killings in Tasmania.
